name: L-theanine
lead: L-theanine is a non-proteinogenic amino acid found mainly in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis) and sold as a supplement for relaxation, focus and sleep, often alongside caffeine [1]. It was identified in green tea in 1949 and isolated from gyokuro leaves in 1950 [1].

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheap way to calm anxiety, improve focus with coffee and sleep better, which proponents tie to better skin, mood and presentation. Small human studies report reduced stress responses and effects on cognition and mood, but regulators and reviews describe the evidence as mixed [1][2][3].

The European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence for claims that theanine improves cognition, reduces stress or supports sleep, and a 2025 review criticized the rigor of much of the literature [1].
infobox: OTC supplement; FDA GRAS in foods up to 250 mg per serving [1]

paras: Theanine makes up about 1 percent of the dry weight of black, green and white tea, and shaded teas such as matcha and gyokuro contain more [1]. It contributes to the umami taste of Japanese green tea [4]. Commercial products may contain some D-form because heat and pH can convert the natural L-form [1].

After oral intake it is absorbed in the small intestine and broken down to glutamate and ethylamine [1]. It weakly binds glutamate receptors, blocking AMPA and kainate and partially activating NMDA receptors in lab work [1]. A small study found an EEG alpha-wave effect for GABA but compared it with theanine in the same experiment [5].

A 2007 study of twelve volunteers found that L-theanine reduced psychological and physiological stress responses to a mental arithmetic task [6]. A 2008 study examined theanine, caffeine and their combination on cognition and mood [7]. A 2017 review covered its metabolism, health effects and safety [8]. In 2011 the EFSA found claims for cognition, stress and sleep unsupported, while a 2020 review suggested 200-400 mg daily might reduce stress during acute stress but judged evidence insufficient for medical use [1].

Safety data are limited. In 2003 Germany's Federal Institute for Risk Assessment objected to adding isolated theanine to drinks, warning of possible effects on psychomotor skills and sedatives [1]. In the US it is sold as a supplement and the FDA considers it generally recognized as safe in foods up to 250 mg per serving; Japan approved its food use in 1964 [1].

Registered studies include a phase 2 trial in boys with ADHD (n=100) [9], a trial of caffeine and theanine on cerebral blood flow, cognition and mood [10], a phase 3 trial in schizophrenia (n=60) [11], and studies in athletes and stressed adults [12]. Published findings include the 2007 stress study [6] and the 2008 cognition study [7]. Reviews in 2024 reported possible benefit over placebo for anxiety, ADHD and schizophrenia symptoms, while a 2025 review criticized unreliable trials [1].

Isolated from gyokuro leaves in Kyoto [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org it is described as a cheap, benign calming supplement used with caffeine.

claims.believers: A poster calls it very cheap and effective, taken before bed or before a test, and says it calms without making you sleepy [13].
claims.experts: A small 2007 study found reduced stress responses, while EFSA found the claim unsupported [6][1].

claims.claim: Combining it with caffeine improves focus.
claims.experts: A 2008 study examined theanine plus caffeine on cognition and mood [7].

claims.claim: It helps focus on low sleep.
claims.believers: A thread asks whether it improves study focus on low sleep, with one reply calling it benign [14].
claims.experts: No studies found on this specific use.

claims.claim: It can backfire in the morning.
claims.believers: One user reports feeling bad taking it in the morning and attributes this to cortisol suppression [13].
claims.experts: No studies found supporting a cortisol mechanism.

card.summary: Tea amino acid used as a cheap calming, focus supplement; small studies show stress effects, regulators call evidence insufficient.
card.note: EFSA found insufficient evidence for sleep, stress and cognition claims.

quick.overview:
L-theanine is an amino acid from tea sold as a calming, focus-boosting supplement, often paired with caffeine.

Small studies report reduced stress responses, but EFSA and recent reviews describe evidence as limited.
quick.mechanism: Resembles glutamate and weakly interacts with glutamate receptors in lab studies.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited; a German agency warned about effects with sedatives. It is OTC in the US and GRAS up to 250 mg per serving in foods.
